task.goal: Produce one slide of a documentary-style 'list carousel' that uses a recognizable real-world case study to illustrate a repeating-pattern argument, alternating full-bleed photo-collage beats with spare text-only 'claim / repeated' refrain beats, and closing on a reflective question that reframes the case study onto the viewer's own situation.
task.success_condition: Photo beats carry a short third-person editorial caption (never a first-person quote from the case study's subject); refrain beats render as a short claim line followed by the word 'repeated' on its own line, with no other decoration; the closing beat is a single open question with no imagery and no answer supplied; nothing in the slide is presented as an official statement from the club, brand, or individuals depicted.
task.atomic_boundary: One source beat becomes one slide: a photo beat, a refrain beat, or the closing reflective question. This harness governs a single slide unit, not which real-world case study is chosen, the underlying photography, or the full carousel's sequencing.

source_expression_moment.description: The single beat for this slide: a photo-caption observation, a refrain claim, or the closing reflective question.

voice_context.description: Tone/voice reference for the beat copy — observational, measured, non-triumphalist; states the pattern rather than celebrating the outcome.

carousel_slide.description: One production-ready portrait slide: either a photo-collage beat with a short caption, a text-only refrain beat, or a text-only closing question, composed per this format's visual syntax.

activative_input.hidden_pressure: The reader assumes recognisable identity is either innate talent or lucky timing; this format has to make the unglamorous, repeated groundwork visible without turning the case study into a highlight reel.
activative_input.stance: Observational, measured, non-triumphalist — states what repeated rather than celebrating a single win.
stakes: the case study reads as a highlight reel instead of a pattern
the closing question gets answered for the reader instead of left open
identity_urges: see my own slow, repeated work as legitimate progress
resist counting only the trophy moment
activative_input.participation_design: The reader follows the alternating photo/refrain rhythm, arrives at the resolution beat, then is handed the closing question with no resolution supplied.
activative_input.intended_reaction: The reader maps the case study's 'repeated small pattern before the big outcome' onto their own current, outcome-less effort.
activative_input.smallest_useful_commitment: Name one thing in your own work that's already being recognised, before the outcome arrives.
wrong_reading_locks: Do not present a beat's caption or claim as a verbatim quote from the case study's subject (club, players, coaching staff, or brand) — the editorial voice here is third-party observational commentary, not an on-the-record statement, and phrasing it as a direct quote misattributes speech to a real organisation or individual.

Do not let a refrain beat ('claim' + 'repeated') stand alone without a preceding photo beat or the closing question bracketing it — the refrain is a rhythmic device that turns a one-off observation into a pattern; isolated, it reads as a stray non-sequitur rather than a chorus.

Do not resolve the closing reflective question with an answer, brand pitch, or CTA in the same slide — the format's mechanism depends on ending on an open question the viewer answers privately about their own situation; supplying the answer collapses it into a generic testimonial ad.

Do not swap a real, identifiable athlete, coach, or fan from the reference specimens for a generic stand-in while keeping the same real-world caption, and do not treat the real people, club crest, and sponsor branding visible in these specimens as cleared for reuse — likeness and trademark clearance for this specific case study is a separate, unresolved question this harness does not settle.

Do not crop out or alter club crests, sponsor logos, or kit branding to 'neutralise' a photo while the caption still names the same real club or event — either use accurately attributed real imagery or fictionalise the case study; a laundered image paired with an unchanged real-world caption misrepresents the source.
